source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: Seven cognitive biases were injected into USMLE questions. Every one of six LLMs lost accuracy. This is the main LLM test of the Croskerry bias list.
numbers: 1,273 MedQA questions, 6 models. No-bias accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7b 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama-13b 33.4%. GPT-3.5 average drop 37.4% across biases.
limits: Bias is injected as a text hint, not a natural error. Multiple choice only. 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: Planted hints (a suggested wrong answer, a recent case, a common-answer claim) hurt weak models a lot. The scaffold should not take a hint in the prompt as evidence.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) BiasMedQA, per-bias effects
finding: Strength of damage depends on the bias type and model. GPT-4 is nearly immune to confirmation bias but weak to false consensus.
numbers: GPT-4 worst case: false consensus, drop of 14.0%. GPT-4 confirmation bias: drop of only 0.2%. Across models the mean drop was largest for false consensus (24.9%), then frequency (18.2%) and recency (12.9%); smallest for confirmation (8.1%).
limits: Averages mix very different models.
agent_relevance: Social-pressure hints ('most doctors say X') are the strongest attack. Guardrail against deferring to claimed consensus is worth more than a generic 'beware bias' line.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) BiasMedQA, mitigation arms
finding: Three prompt fixes were tested: a short bias-education warning, a one-shot bad-example, and a few-shot good/bad example. Gains were real only for GPT-4 and were partial. Weaker models gained little or got worse.
numbers: GPT-4 education: frequency bias 0.627 to 0.720. GPT-4 one-shot: recency 0.679 to 0.742. GPT-4 few-shot raised no-bias accuracy to 0.757 and status quo to 0.770. Mixtral and GPT-3.5 only marginal under education. Authors say gains were 'minor'.
limits: Safety filters made text-bison refuse 94.4% (one-shot) and 99.5% (few-shot) of items, so those rows are unreliable. Single run, no CIs.
agent_relevance: The LLM version of 'awareness does little' holds for weaker models; worked examples beat plain warnings. Spend effort on examples of correct handling, not on exhortation.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: A 13,465-prompt test of anchoring, framing, group attribution, primacy and status quo in GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2 (7B, 13B). A new method, self-help, has the model rewrite its own prompt to remove bias. It worked best.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; 400 per experiment in the main tables. GPT-4 framing gap: admits 40.5% more students under reject framing (0.375 vs 0.780); with self-help the gap fell to 0.01 (0.270 vs 0.280). Self-help cut biased prompts to 0% for Llama-2 13B and 6% for Llama-2 7B (group attribution).
quote: few-shot prompting can lead to failure cases
limits: Student-admission and similar proxy tasks, not medicine. Small subset per cell.
agent_relevance: A 'rewrite the question neutrally before answering' step (debias the input) beats telling the model to be careful. Fits the idea of a pre-answer cleanup state.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) BiasBuster, awareness and few-shot arms
finding: Awareness prompts gave small gains. Contrastive and counterfactual few-shot examples often broke the task: the model answered always yes or always no.
numbers: Llama-2 7B contrastive: admit 0.996 vs reject 1.000. Counterfactual 0.542 vs 0.000. GPT-3.5 awareness helped primacy mildly. Anchoring: awareness helped Llama; few-shot examples led to failure cases.
limits: Table is hard to parse in text extraction; read as direction, not exact values.
agent_relevance: Debiasing text can wreck instruction following. Any added forcing step must be tested for collapse to one answer, not only for bias.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: GPT-4 and GPT-4o were anchored by hints from a fake expert or an irrelevant number on 62 forecasting questions. Chain of thought, thoughts of principles, ignore-the-hint and reflection all failed to remove the effect.
numbers: 62 questions, three hints each (fact, two anchors). Four strategies tested; t-tests still significant with very small p-values. A 'both anchors' strategy (give two opposing hints) brought GPT-4 near the bias-free value on 8 of the expert-hint questions shown.
quote: simple algorithms such as Chain-of-Thought, Thoughts of Principles, Ignoring Anchor Hints, and Reflection are not sufficient
limits: Not medical. Numeric forecast answers. Small school-based authorship; GPT-4 family only.
agent_relevance: Strong LLM match to the Norman finding: slow-down and ignore-it instructions fail. Gathering opposing evidence (a forced counter-anchor) works better. Supports operator 'seek disconfirming input'.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy through Multi-Agent Conversations: Using LLMs to Mitigate Cognitive Bias
finding: GPT-4 Turbo agents played junior resident, devil's advocate, senior tutor and recorder on 16 case reports where bias caused a human misdiagnosis. The discussion lifted accuracy from 0 to 71.3%.
numbers: 16 cases x 5 runs = 80 simulations. Initial diagnosis 0/80 (cases were chosen because the first answer was wrong). After discussion: top diagnosis 57/80 (71.3%); top two 64/80 (80.0%).
limits: No control arm (single model asked to reconsider). Cases selected for first-answer failure, so 0% start is by design. Possible training-data overlap; one unpublished case added to check. Text only.
agent_relevance: A role-based cognitive forcing design (devil's advocate plus premature-closure tutor) is already used in an LLM loop, but the gain is not separated from just 'think again'.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Silence is Not Consensus: Catfish Agent
finding: Multi-agent medical LLM teams often converge without debate (silent agreement). A dissent agent that challenges early consensus cut silent agreement and raised accuracy on 9 medical Q&A and 3 VQA sets.
numbers: Silent rate: MedAgents 64.0% (MedQA) and 89.0% (PubMedQA); MDAgents 61.0% and 61.0%; Catfish 17.0% and 11.0%. Of failures, silent agreement: MedAgents 61.9%/90.7%, MDAgents 68.1%/64.0%, Catfish 18.0%/14.3%. Average +12.7 points on Q&A (39.2% relative gain over DeepSeek-R1). Ablation on one hard set: no catfish 36.0%, catfish in team only 44.0%, with tone design 45.0%.
limits: Benchmarks are multiple choice. Gains versus other frameworks, not versus a plain 'reconsider' prompt. Authors' own metric for silent agreement.
agent_relevance: The LLM form of premature closure is group agreement without critique. A structured dissent step, tuned to case difficulty, is a tested forcing function. Tone matters (critique without derailing).

source: Handler, Bedi and Shah (2026) Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs
finding: Five frontier models (including GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek R1, Grok 3) usually pick an answer when the correct option is removed. A safety prompt telling them to abstain, clarify or escalate cut this but left most of it.
numbers: MedQA n=500 (250 intact, 250 no-valid-option); AfriMed-QA n=490. Mean false action about 70% on both; with safety prompt about 48% on both. Per model baseline 55-81% (MedQA). Without Grok 3, intact accuracy fell only 1.0 point. DeepSeek R1 dropped 24 (MedQA) and 26 points (AfriMed); Gemini 2.5 Pro only 55% to 48%. HealthBench 861 items: baseline premature closure 20.7% (GPT-5.4) to 44.6% (R1); safety prompt cut 4.2-7.9 points. 191 adversarial queries: baseline 59.3% (Opus 4.7) to 91.4% (R1).
limits: Preprint. Single prompt wording. Grok 3 lost accuracy on answerable items (overcorrection). Abstention is a proxy for closure.
agent_relevance: A direct 'check whether information is enough' instruction helps measurably but leaves a large residue. Needs an explicit sufficiency check state and a cost test on answerable items.

source: Fang et al. (2026) MINT: Benchmarking Multi-turn Medical Diagnosis: Hold, Lure, and Self-Correction
finding: On 1,035 cases split into evidence shards, 11 LLMs answered too early, even when told to wait. Holding the question back until later turns helped a lot. Lab results acted as a lure that triggered early answers.
numbers: 1,035 cases, 11 LLMs. Over 55% of answers committed in first two turns. Deferring the diagnostic question raised first-commit accuracy by up to 62.6%. Guess rate when told to WAIT: Med42-70B 99.9%, GPT-5-mini 5.9%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 3.7%. Reserving salient evidence for later prevented a drop of up to 23.3%. Wrong-to-right revisions up to 10.6 times the rate of right-to-wrong.
quote: Prompting alone cannot reliably suppress early answering
limits: Preprint; cases built from MedQA-style vignettes by Qwen3-32B sharding. 'Wait' is a prompt, not a structural block.
agent_relevance: Slow down by instruction fails for weaker models; slow down by structure (hide the question until evidence is in) works. Strong case for ordering information rather than telling the agent to be patient. Revision up is easier than commit down.

source: Srivastava et al. (2026) Agentic AI-based Framework for Mitigating Premature Diagnostic Handoff and Silent Hallucination
finding: A hard checklist gate (OLDCARTS history items must be complete before diagnosis) plus 5 samples with a semantic-entropy check improved accuracy over an unconstrained agent. The gate alone did not.
numbers: llama-3.1-70b-instruct, MedQA vignettes, simulated patient. N=150: baseline 38.0% accuracy, gate only (K=1) 32.7% (-5.3), full gate plus K=5 samples 49.3% (+11.3). Completeness 2.4/8 (30%) baseline vs 6.667/8 full. At N=50: 34.0 / 30.0 / 56.0. Entropy vs completeness r=-0.181, p=0.027 at N=150 (r=-0.008, p=0.954 at N=50).
limits: One mid-size model; simulated patients; narrow checklist; the judge is an LLM; the gate-only drop is not tested for significance.
agent_relevance: A mandatory checklist gate did NOT raise accuracy by itself; it raised completeness only. The accuracy gain came from sampling and disagreement checking. Matches human finding that checklists alone are weak.

source: Watanabe et al. (2026) When to Stop Asking: Factor Coverage Bias
finding: LLMs treat the amount of relevant information as a cue that a case is decidable, even when the missing facts could still change the answer. This is a model form of premature closure. More reasoning effort did not fix it.
numbers: Benchmark of 1,080 pairs from clinical scoring systems. Adding a relevant factor raised the chance the augmented case is judged determinable even if it stayed undeterminable; effect persisted with higher reasoning effort. Adding irrelevant text of equal length lowered it, and reasoning mostly removed that effect.
limits: Scoring-system cases; open-weight and proprietary models mixed; exact per-model rates not extracted from the text.
agent_relevance: Thinking longer fixes length noise but not closure from partial but relevant evidence. The scaffold needs a 'could any missing item flip the answer' test, not only a long reasoning pass.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of LLMs in agentic clinical reasoning
finding: 32 frontier models had to request data over three rounds in hematologic oncology. Errors were mostly search satisficing, anchoring and premature closure. Reasoning text looked good but did not track accuracy.
numbers: 32 models; best overall accuracy 68%. Information utilization predicted accuracy (R=0.69, P<0.001). Utilization fell from 57% to 26% in the final round. 91% of reasoning traces scored above rubric threshold but were decorrelated from accuracy.
limits: One specialty; rubric scored by model/rater pipeline; preprint.
agent_relevance: Fluent reasoning is not a sign of debiasing. Measure information use and stopping, not the quality of the written rationale.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Asking a model to review and fix its own answer without outside feedback does not help and often hurts. It is the LLM analogue of 'stop and reflect'.
numbers: GPT-3.5: CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one self-correction round (41.8 after two); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (74.7); HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. With oracle labels (told when to stop) GSM8K reached 95.5 (GPT-3.5) and 97.5 (GPT-4). GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Reasoning benchmarks, not diagnosis; 2023 models; GPT-4 intrinsic numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Generic reflect-and-revise is not a debiasing tool. Use outside checks (tests, a second independent sample, retrieved facts). This agrees with Norman's review that slowing down alone gave nothing.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic Reasoning Prompts Reveal the Potential for LLM Interpretability in Medicine
finding: Prompts copying clinician methods (differential diagnosis, analytic, intuitive, Bayesian reasoning) did not reduce accuracy in GPT-4 and gave no clear gain over plain chain of thought. In GPT-3.5 some made it worse.
numbers: MedQA. GPT-4 chain of thought 76%; intuitive 77% (+0.8, P=0.73); differential diagnosis 78% (+2.2, P=0.24); analytic 78% (+1.6, P=0.35); Bayesian 72% (-3.4, P=0.07). GPT-3.5 chain of thought 46%; differential diagnosis 38% (P<0.001); analytic 40% (P=0.001); Bayesian 42% (P=0.02); intuitive 48% (P=0.9).
limits: Multiple-choice MedQA; the aim was interpretability, not bias reduction.
agent_relevance: Forcing a differential or Bayesian write-up gives a readable rationale at no gain in accuracy for strong models and a loss for weak ones. Use it for audit, not for accuracy.

source: Alessa et al. (2025) Quantifying Cognitive Bias Induction in LLM-Generated Content
finding: LLMs are also bias sources: summaries change sentiment, stress early text and hallucinate after the knowledge cutoff. 18 mitigation methods were compared; no single fix worked for all bias types.
numbers: Averaged over models: framing change in 26.42% of cases; hallucination on 60.33% of post-cutoff questions; primacy in 10.12%. Humans 32% more likely to buy after an LLM summary. Mirostat decoding cut primacy for Phi-3 (5.4% to 4.2%) but raised it for Llama-3-8B (7.0% to 15.5%). Position-invariant shuffle raised coverage (0.843 to 0.891) but raised primacy to 11.5% and framing change to 21.2%. Self-awareness prompt coverage 0.889.
limits: Summaries and news fact-checking, not diagnosis. Small model set.
agent_relevance: Fixes trade one bias for another. A scaffold should check several bias metrics at once. Primacy of early text matters when order of case facts is fixed.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) BiasMedQA, limits and method note
finding: The authors note that 5.3% of USMLE items lack enough information for a clear decision, and that models rarely say so. They also state that bias gains from mitigation are modest and should reach the accuracy of a no-bias run.
numbers: Mitigation arm: GPT-4 no-bias accuracy 0.727 baseline vs 0.763 (one-shot) and 0.757 (few-shot), so the example itself changes plain accuracy.
limits: The shift in no-bias accuracy under examples may be partly format effect, not debiasing.
agent_relevance: Test any debiasing prompt on unbiased items too; some of the gain is generic prompt help.

source: Ke et al. (2024) multi-agent conversation, role design
finding: The junior resident agent was told to make swift assumptions, the second resident to challenge anchoring and confirmation, the senior to name biases and prevent premature closure. A recorder lists differentials.
numbers: 4 agents built on AutoGen with GPT-4 Turbo; each of 16 scenarios run 5 times. Case 12 pneumothorax missed by human clinicians was found by the agents.
limits: Authors state published case reports limit generality, no images, and LLM pretraining biases may remain.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete prompt layout for a bias-aware critique step: one role to attack the first answer, one to name the bias, one to log alternatives.

source: Handler et al. (2026) Premature closure, open-ended tests
finding: Closure was worst where cues of danger were absent. Models gave advice on underspecified low-risk questions at baseline 73.2% (GPT-5.4) to 96.1% (DeepSeek R1), but much less on underspecified urgent questions (5.0-35.8%).
numbers: 861 HealthBench questions. Safety prompt: Grok 3 24.3% to 16.4% overall; urgent underspecified: Grok 3 19.6% to 6.1%, Claude Opus 4.7 12.3% to 4.5%. Rubric scores rose only 1-3 points (GPT-5.4 60.9% to 62.6%). On sufficient-context control questions, clarification rate stayed 3.5%.
limits: Rubric scoring by an LLM grader; preprint.
agent_relevance: Models respond to danger cues, not to missing information. A check that asks 'what is missing' must fire even without alarming cues.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Catfish Agent, complexity-aware design
finding: The dissent agent fires more on hard cases and uses a calibrated tone. A chi-square test showed silent agreement was linked to failure in both baseline frameworks.
numbers: chi-square(1)=5.345, p=0.0208 for MDAgents; chi-square(1)=5.896 for MedAgents. Harder sets: the catfish method reached 32.0% on one hard set where MedAgents scored 3.0% and MDAgents 9.0%; 50.0% vs 8.0% on MMLU-Pro (4o).
limits: Strong baselines were chosen from the same paper family; hard-set samples are small.
agent_relevance: Gate the forcing step by case difficulty to avoid wasted calls and over-challenge on easy cases.

source: Fang et al. (2026) MINT, self-correction finding
finding: Models do correct themselves when new evidence arrives: wrong-to-right changes were up to 10.6 times as common as right-to-wrong. Premature commitment wastes this ability.
numbers: Holding longer raised accuracy by 11.7% in one comparison. Lab-result lure analysed on MedQA cases with labs, n=249, across 10-turn settings with lab shard at turns 2, 5 or 10.
limits: Preprint; accuracy at first commitment is a defined metric of this paper.
agent_relevance: Revision after new evidence is safe; revision after only more thought (Huang 2023) is not. Keep the loop open for new facts, not for more self-review.

source: Srivastava et al. (2026) premature-handoff agent, semantic entropy
finding: Five independent diagnostic samples were pooled; the answer counted correct if the truth was in the pooled set. Disagreement was measured by semantic entropy.
numbers: K=5 samples; mean semantic entropy about 0.93; MAX_TRIAGE_TURNS=15; Llama-3.1-70B; N=50,100,150 cases (nested). Accuracy 56.0%, 47.0%, 49.3%.
limits: Pooled-set scoring is more lenient than top-1; the K=1 baseline is scored on one answer, so the gain partly reflects scoring.
agent_relevance: Part of the +11.3 gain may be the scoring rule (any of 5 answers counts). Compare at equal answer budget before copying.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) BiasBuster, GPT-4 and primacy/anchoring
finding: All models prefer options listed first (A or B over C or D), like primacy. Self-help flattens this to a more even spread. The status-quo hint often reversed (model avoided the suggested default).
numbers: Status-quo-biased prompts inversely biased every model except GPT-4. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math (group attribution). Anchoring sequential setup vs all-at-once: models changed 52% of decisions when allowed to revise.
limits: Student-ranking tasks; not clinical. Percentages as stated in text.
agent_relevance: Randomise option order and test for a letter-position effect before trusting any multiple-choice diagnosis score.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring, dataset design
finding: Questions came from a prediction game with human anchoring data. Hints were a fact, an expert-opinion anchor and an irrelevant anchor. Both expert-style and irrelevant anchors moved answers.
numbers: 62 questions in several domains; GPT-4 and GPT-4o; four prompt mitigations compared with plain prompt by t-test.
limits: Compared only a single prompt per strategy; temperature and sample counts not extracted.
agent_relevance: Even a hint labelled from an 'expert' with no evidence moves a strong model. Strip authority labels from retrieved or user text before reasoning.

source: Savage et al. (2024) diagnostic reasoning prompts, design
finding: Prompts were built from clinical methods: differential diagnosis formation, intuitive reasoning, analytic reasoning and Bayesian inference. They produced a written rationale the clinician can check.
numbers: Inter-rater agreement on grading 97% (kappa 0.93) for GPT-3.5 and 99% for GPT-4 on MedQA.
limits: Rationales were judged for plausibility, not for being the true cause of the answer (faithfulness not shown).
agent_relevance: A rationale can look right without being the reason. Do not use it as proof that bias was avoided.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) agentic clinical reasoning, utilization
finding: Models stopped requesting data in the last round, exactly when molecular and cytogenetic data were needed. This is satisficing, a cognitive-forcing target.
numbers: Utilization 57% falling to 26% in final round; R=0.69 with accuracy; best of 32 models 68%.
limits: Only hematologic oncology; static case bank.
agent_relevance: A forced 'list what is not yet checked' step before commit directly targets this.

source: Watanabe et al. (2026) Factor coverage bias, benchmark design
finding: Pairs of cases were built so adding a decision-relevant factor to either side leaves determinability unchanged. A control with irrelevant text of the same length separates a closure bias from a length effect.
numbers: 1,080 pairs; reasoning effort varied via OpenRouter models.
limits: Pairs built from scoring systems that have exact thresholds; real cases are fuzzier.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean test for our own stop rule: add relevant but non-decisive facts and see if the agent wrongly stops.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Cannot Self-Correct, why it fails
finding: The model cannot judge whether its own reasoning is right, so a review step flips correct answers as often as wrong ones. Oracle stopping gives large gains that real use does not have.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5 standard 75.9 vs oracle self-correct 95.5; GPT-4 84.3 vs 97.5; CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 75.8 vs oracle 82.0; HotpotQA GPT-3.5 26.0 vs oracle 49.0.
limits: Gap shown is the value of correct feedback, not of the method.
agent_relevance: Debiasing steps need a reliable signal of when to change. Without it, the forcing step is noise.
